1A1.why: IMO describes the GMDSS as a worldwide network of automated emergency communications for ships at sea, using satellite as well as terrestrial radio techniques to alert rescue authorities and nearby ships. It isn't a commercial-communications system or a collision-avoidance system, and it covers far more than DSC.

src.quote: is essentially a worldwide network of automated emergency communications for ships at sea
can be rapidly alerted through satellite and terrestrial communication techniques to a distress incident

1A2.why: The GMDSS exists to automate and improve emergency (distress and safety) communications for the world's shipping. It is a worldwide network of automated emergency communications, not a system for company or low-cost communications. Overall SAR coordination rests with rescue coordination centres ashore, although ships take part in the search.

src.quote: is essentially a worldwide network of automated emergency communications for ships at sea
the whole operation is co-ordinated by a designated rescue co-ordination centre

1A3.why: The GMDSS is shore-centred: search and rescue authorities ashore are alerted to the distress, and ships in the vicinity can then be brought in to help in a coordinated search and rescue operation. Alerts don't depend on chains of DSC relays or on reports from nearby ships.

src.quote: The basic concept of the GMDSS is that search and rescue authorities ashore, as well as shipping in the immediate vicinity of the ship in distress, will be rapidly alerted to a distress incident so they can assist in a co-ordinated search and rescue operation with the minimum of delay.

1A4.why: At its core the GMDSS links search and rescue authorities ashore with ships in the immediate vicinity of a ship in distress, so both are alerted and can work together. VHF DSC, MF/HF radiotelephony and narrow-band direct printing are only some of the tools it uses.

src.quote: The basic concept of the GMDSS is that search and rescue authorities ashore, as well as shipping in the immediate vicinity of the ship in distress, will be rapidly alerted to a distress incident so they can assist in a co-ordinated search and rescue operation with the minimum of delay.

1A5.why: Under the GMDSS, every ship must be able to perform the communication functions considered essential for its own safety and the safety of other ships in the area, wherever it operates. The other choices are wrong: ships don't automatically relay DSC distress alerts or acknowledge every alert.

src.quote: every ship will be able, irrespective of the area in which it operates, to perform those communication functions considered essential for the safety of the ship itself and of other ships operating in the same area.

1A6.why: The GMDSS rules (Part 80, Subpart W, which implements SOLAS) apply to all passenger ships regardless of size and to cargo ships of 300 gross tonnage and upwards. The keyed answer names the cargo-ship threshold; small coastal vessels under 300 gross tons aren't covered.

src.quote: apply to all passenger ships regardless of size and cargo ships of 300 tons gross tonnage and upwards

2A1.why: Terrestrial radio means ordinary radio between ships and shore stations, without satellites. VHF, MF and HF DSC are terrestrial systems. Inmarsat-FBB and Inmarsat-C are satellite systems, and GPS is satellite navigation.

src.quote: Although satellites play an important part in the GMDSS, terrestrial radio is still important.

2A2.why: Inmarsat-C is a satellite communication system: it works through Inmarsat's geostationary satellites. VHF, MF and HF are terrestrial radio, NAVTEX is a terrestrial MF broadcast, and a SART is a radar transponder.

src.quote: within the coverage of an INMARSAT geostationary satellite in which continuous alerting is available

2A3.why: The ship's satellite EPIRB must be able to be carried by one person into a survival craft and must float free and activate automatically if the ship sinks, so it is used in or near the survival craft. NAVTEX and a fathometer are bridge equipment, and COSPAS-SARSAT is the satellite system, not a piece of equipment on board.

src.quote: capable of being carried by one person into a survival craft, capable of floating free if the ship sinks and of being automatically activated when afloat

2A4.why: The DSC controller is the unit you program to send DSC calls: distress alerts as well as calls to individual stations. A DSC scanning watch receiver only listens, NAVTEX only receives broadcasts, and GPS supplies position.

src.quote: The distress signal is a digital selective call using an internationally recognized distress call format

2A5.why: GMDSS equipment that sends automatic distress alerts needs the ship's position, which comes from a navigation receiver, in practice GPS, either built in or connected. COSPAS-SARSAT and EPIRBs are for alerting, and Inmarsat-F77 is a communications terminal.

src.quote: must have either an integral navigation receiver or capability of being connected to an external navigation receiver

2A6.why: NAVTEX is the receiver that picks up international broadcasts of maritime safety information (navigational and weather warnings), and every GMDSS ship must carry one. SARTs and EPIRBs are locating and alerting devices, and Inmarsat-F77 is a voice and data terminal.

src.quote: A receiver capable of receiving international NAVTEX service broadcasts

3A1.why: Sea area A4 is defined as everything outside sea areas A1, A2 and A3. In practice that means the polar regions, beyond the coverage of geostationary satellites.

src.quote: Sea area A4. An area outside sea areas A1, A2 and A3.

3A2.why: Sea area A2 is the area, excluding A1, within radiotelephone coverage of at least one MF coast station with continuous DSC alerting.

src.quote: Sea area A2. An area, excluding sea area A1, within the radiotelephone coverage of at least one MF coast station in which continuous DSC alerting is available

3A3.why: A ship that always stays within range of a VHF coast station with continuous DSC alerting is operating in sea area A1.

src.quote: Sea area A1. An area within the radiotelephone coverage of at least one VHF coast station in which continuous DSC alerting is available

3A4.why: Sea area A3 is the area, excluding A1 and A2, within coverage of an Inmarsat geostationary satellite with continuous alerting. AOR-E, AOR-W, POR and IOR are names of Inmarsat ocean regions, not sea areas.

src.quote: Sea area A3. An area, excluding sea areas A1 and A2, within the coverage of an INMARSAT geostationary satellite in which continuous alerting is available.

3A5.why: Ships equipped for sea area A3 by the MF/HF option, and ships equipped for A4, must carry an MF/HF installation that works on DSC, radiotelephony and narrow-band direct printing (SITOR/NBDP). In A3 the Inmarsat option can be used instead, which is why NBDP is a partial or alternative requirement. Ships that stay in A1 or A2 don't need it.

src.quote: An MF/HF radio installation capable of transmitting and receiving on all distress and safety frequencies in the bands between 1605-27500 kHz using DSC, radiotelephony, and narrow-band direct-printing telegraphy
ships engaged on voyages in all sea areas must be provided with the radio installations and equipment required by § 80.1091(b)

3A6.why: That is the definition of sea area A1: within the radiotelephone coverage of at least one VHF coast station with continuous DSC alerting.

src.quote: Sea area A1. An area within the radiotelephone coverage of at least one VHF coast station in which continuous DSC alerting is available as defined by the International Maritime Organization.

4A1.why: GMDSS equipment requirements depend on the sea areas the ship will pass through on its intended voyage. The operator choices are wrong: every compulsory ship needs at least two GMDSS radio operators, in every sea area, and no rule requires a maintainer specifically for A3 and A4.

src.quote: as appropriate for the sea area of areas through which it will pass during its intended voyage
Ships must carry at least two persons holding GMDSS Radio Operator's Licenses

4A2.why: Ships must be able to perform the GMDSS functions (distress alerting, maritime safety information, general communications and so on) throughout their intended voyage, with equipment chosen for the sea areas they'll actually be in. They don't need equipment for sea areas they won't enter.

src.quote: capable of complying with the functional requirements prescribed by § 80.1081 throughout its intended voyage
Of transmitting and receiving maritime safety information

4A3.why: The GMDSS functional requirements are distress alerting, search and rescue coordinating communications, on-scene communications, locating signals, maritime safety information, general radiocommunications and bridge-to-bridge communications. Choice D lists only items from that list. The others include things that aren't GMDSS functions, such as relaying satellite alerts or direction-finding EPIRB signals.

src.quote: Of transmitting and receiving search and rescue co-ordinating communications;
Of transmitting and receiving on-scene communications;
Of transmitting and receiving bridge-to-bridge communications.

4A4.why: Maritime safety information reaches ships by NAVTEX, by the Inmarsat enhanced group call system (SafetyNET), or by HF direct-printing telegraphy (NBDP) broadcasts. Inmarsat-F77 and VHF weather channels aren't GMDSS MSI systems.

src.quote: A receiver capable of receiving international NAVTEX service broadcasts
a radio facility for reception of maritime safety information by the INMARSAT enhanced group calling system

4A5.why: Bridge-to-bridge communications, general radiocommunications and search and rescue communications are all GMDSS functional requirements. Weather-fax reception, company email and VHF weather channels are not.

src.quote: Of transmitting and receiving search and rescue co-ordinating communications;
Of transmitting and receiving general radiocommunications to and from shore-based radio sytsems or networks; and
Of transmitting and receiving bridge-to-bridge communications.

4A6.why: Transmitting and receiving locating signals, general radiocommunications and SAR communications are all GMDSS functional requirements. The other choices go wrong: ships must be able to alert by at least two separate means (not one), and ships receive MSI rather than sending it by EGC.

src.quote: Of transmitting and receiving signals for locating;
by at least two separate and independent means, each using a different radiocommunication service

5A1.why: A ship that stays in sea area A1 must have a radio installation that can start a ship-to-shore distress alert from the position where the ship is normally navigated. That is the requirement itself, so A is the answer. The rule lets it be met in several ways (VHF DSC, the 406 MHz EPIRB, MF DSC within MF DSC coast coverage, HF DSC or Inmarsat), so C describes allowed options rather than the requirement. B is wrong because every GMDSS ship also carries a 406 MHz satellite EPIRB, so VHF DSC is never its only alerting means. D describes the old 2182 kHz alarm system.

src.quote: must be provided with a radio installation capable of initiating the transmission of ship-to-shore distress alerts from the position from which the ship is normally navigated
On MF using DSC if the ship is engaged on voyages within coverage of MF coast stations equipped with DSC; or
A satellite emergency position-indicating radio beacon (satellite EPIRB)

5A1.note: Choice C is partly true: the rule does allow MF or HF DSC to meet the A1 alerting requirement. The exam keys A because it states the requirement itself.

5A2.why: Cargo ships of 300 to 500 gross tons need at least one search and rescue locating device (radar transponder or AIS-SART). Every passenger ship and every cargo ship of 500 gross tons and upwards needs one on each side, so a second radar transponder is the extra requirement.

src.quote: At least one radar transponder or AIS-SART (collectively, “search and rescue locating devices”) must be carried on each side of every passenger ship and every cargo ship of 500 tons gross tonnage and upwards.
At least one search and rescue locating device must be carried on every cargo ship of 300 tons gross tonnage and upwards but less than 500 tons gross tonnage.

5A3.why: Ships equipped for sea area A3 choose between two options: an Inmarsat ship earth station plus MF, or an MF/HF installation with HF DSC. Either way, they carry Inmarsat or HF equipment, or both. A4 ships need HF because Inmarsat's geostationary satellites don't cover the polar regions.

src.quote: Ships fitting in accordance to this section have the option to comply with either the requirements of paragraph (a) or (b) of this section.
An INMARSAT ship earth station capable of:
An MF/HF radio installation capable of transmitting and receiving on all distress and safety frequencies

5A4.why: The GMDSS deliberately combines different subsystems, so a ship can send a distress alert by at least two separate and independent means, each using a different radio service. If one fails, another still works. It isn't full duplication of every function, and it isn't about matching national rules.

src.quote: by at least two separate and independent means, each using a different radiocommunication service

5A5.why: Every GMDSS ship needs NAVTEX. A ship that sails in an area with Inmarsat coverage but no international NAVTEX service must also be able to receive maritime safety information by the Inmarsat enhanced group call system (SafetyNET). The exception is a ship that can receive an HF direct-printing (NBDP) MSI service where one is provided.

src.quote: If the ship is engaged on voyages in any area of INMARSAT coverage in which an international NAVTEX service is not provided, a radio facility for reception of maritime safety information by the INMARSAT enhanced group calling system

5A6.why: Every passenger ship and every cargo ship of 500 gross tons and upwards must carry at least three two-way VHF survival craft radiotelephones (SCTs) and two search and rescue locating devices (SARTs), one on each side. Cargo ships of 300 to 500 gross tons need only two SCTs and one SART.

src.quote: At least three two-way VHF radiotelephone apparatus must be provided on every passenger ship and on every cargo ship of 500 tons gross tonnage and upwards.
must be carried on each side of every passenger ship and every cargo ship of 500 tons gross tonnage and upwards

6A1.why: Statement D is false. With shore-based maintenance, repairs must be completed and performance verified before the ship leaves the first port of call after a failure, and every GMDSS unit must be tested before departure from every port, foreign or not. The other statements are true: A1/A2 ships need one maintenance method and A3/A4 ships need two.

src.quote: Maintenance services must be completed and performance verified and noted in the ship's record before departure from the first port of call entered after any failure occurs.
On ships engaged on voyages in sea areas A3 and A4, the availability must be ensured by using a combination of at least two of the following methods

6A2.why: The three GMDSS maintenance methods are duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance and at-sea electronic maintenance capability. How many a ship needs depends on its sea areas (one for A1/A2, two for A3/A4), not on its tonnage.

src.quote: the availability must be ensured by duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance, or at-sea electronic maintenance capability, or a combination of these

6A3.why: A ship that stays within range of MF DSC shore stations is in sea areas A1 and A2, where any one of the three maintenance methods (duplication, shore-based or at-sea) is enough.

src.quote: On ships engaged on voyages in sea areas A1 and A2, the availability must be ensured by duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance, or at-sea electronic maintenance capability, or a combination of these.

6A5.why: Ships in sea areas A3 and A4 must use at least two of the three maintenance methods: duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance, or at-sea maintenance.

src.quote: On ships engaged on voyages in sea areas A3 and A4, the availability must be ensured by using a combination of at least two of the following methods: duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance, or at-sea electronic maintenance capability.

6A6.why: Ships in sea areas A1 and A2 need only one of the three maintenance methods: duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance or at-sea maintenance.

src.quote: On ships engaged on voyages in sea areas A1 and A2, the availability must be ensured by duplication of equipment, shore-based maintenance, or at-sea electronic maintenance capability, or a combination of these.

13C1.why: A GMDSS ship's required equipment must be inspected at least once every 12 months. Under Part 80 the inspection is done on the FCC's behalf by an FCC-licensed technician holding a GMDSS Radio Maintainer's License, who issues the Safety Certificate. It isn't a Coast Guard inspection, and there's no six-month rule or waiver for on-board maintainers.

src.quote: Ships must have the required equipment inspected at least once every 12 months by an FCC-licensed technician holding a GMDSS Radio Maintainer's License.

13C2.why: The required equipment must be inspected at least once every 12 months by an FCC-licensed technician holding a GMDSS Radio Maintainer's License.

src.quote: Ships must have the required equipment inspected at least once every 12 months by an FCC-licensed technician holding a GMDSS Radio Maintainer's License.

13C3.why: Statement C is false: the required equipment must be inspected at least once every 12 months, not every five years. The others are true: single-voyage exemptions are allowed in exceptional circumstances, the rules cover all passenger ships and cargo ships of 300 gross tons and up, and two licensed GMDSS radio operators are required.

src.quote: Ships must have the required equipment inspected at least once every 12 months
In exceptional circumstances, for a single voyage outside the sea area or sea areas for which the ship is equipped.

13C4.why: Statement D is false: a partial or conditional exemption can be granted, in exceptional circumstances, for a single voyage outside the sea areas the ship is equipped for. The other statements are true.

src.quote: partial or conditional exemptions may be granted to individual ships
In exceptional circumstances, for a single voyage outside the sea area or sea areas for which the ship is equipped.

13C5.why: An inspector checks the station as a whole: required documents and publications may have to be shown, operators may be asked to demonstrate the equipment, and the ship has to be able to perform all its distress and safety functions. Equipment that isn't working can't simply wait for the next port, and outdated publications don't count just because new ones are on order.

src.quote: a ship must not depart from any port unless and until the ship is capable of performing all distress and safety functions

13C6.why: A foreign government may ask to see the ship station license. It may inspect the radio installation when the license can't be produced without delay or when irregularities are observed, such as required equipment found not working. Simply visiting a port for the first time isn't a reason for an inspection.

src.quote: When the license cannot be produced without delay or when irregularities are observed, Governments or administrations may inspect the radio installations

14C1.why: The manufacturer's operating manuals explain how to set up and use each piece of GMDSS equipment, and Part 80 requires them to be on board. Part 80 Subpart W sets the requirements but doesn't explain how to operate a particular radio.

src.quote: all manufacturers' instruction manuals and maintenance manuals for each piece of equipment required and installed must be available on-board ship

14C2.why: The FCC's GMDSS rules for U.S. ships are in 47 CFR Part 80, Subpart W. CCIR Recommendation 476 is an old technical standard for NBDP (SITOR) equipment, not a set of regulations, and the FCC's shipboard rules are in Part 80, not Part 83. The Coast Guard doesn't issue the FCC's radio rules.

src.quote: The regulations contained within this subpart apply to all passenger ships regardless of size and cargo ships of 300 tons gross tonnage and upwards.

14C3.why: The GMDSS distress, urgency and safety procedures for U.S. ships are in 47 CFR Part 80 Subpart W, which also defines what counts as distress traffic. Manufacturers' manuals explain the equipment, not the procedures, and Part 90 covers land mobile radio.

src.quote: Distress traffic consists of all messages relating to the immediate assistance required by the ship in distress, including search and rescue communications and on-scene communications.

14C4.why: The FCC's station-documents table requires cargo ships of 300 tons and up to carry the station license, station logs, operator authorizations, the Part 80 rules, ITU service publications (including the lists of ship and coast stations), and the ITU Manual for Use by the Maritime Mobile and Maritime Mobile-Satellite Services. D is wrong because the manual is an ITU publication, not an IMO one. A and B each include one acceptable item (the GMDSS Master Plan or NGA Pub. 117, either of which satisfies the rule), but they also list an Inmarsat handbook or IAMSAR Volume III, which aren't in the FCC's table.

src.quote: Cargo ships (300 tons and up): Station License R(1); Appropriate Operator Authorization R; Station Logs R;
Part 80; FCC Rules and Regulations R;
Manual for Use by Maritime Mobile (M/M) Service and M/M Satellite Service R
The requirements for having the GMDSS Master Plan, NGA Publication 117, Admiralty List of Radio Signals or IMO Circ. 7 are satisfied by having any one of those four documents.

14C5.why: The FCC's station-documents table requires these ships to carry the ITU List of Coast Stations (List IV), the List of Ship Stations (List V), the appropriate Safety Convention certificate, and the ITU Manual for Use by the Maritime Mobile and Maritime Mobile-Satellite Services. The "ITU Master Plan" doesn't exist (the GMDSS Master Plan is an IMO publication), and the manual is from the ITU, not the IMO.

src.quote: Appropriate Safety Convention Certificate R;
List of Ship Stations R(6); Manual for Use by Maritime Mobile (M/M) Service and M/M Satellite Service R; List of Coast Stations R(5);

14C6.why: The ITU's List of Ship Stations and Maritime Mobile Service Identity Assignments (List V) contains the ship station details, including MMSIs, that administrations notify to the ITU, so you can look up a vessel from its MMSI.

src.quote: The List of Ship Stations and Maritime Mobile Service Identity Assignments (List V) is a service publication containing data collected from Administrations by the Radiocommunication Bureau

15C1.why: A GMDSS Radio Operator's License covers operating the station and basic equipment adjustments. Any adjustment or servicing that may affect the station's proper operation, such as aligning a transmitter's output stage, must be done by or under a qualified GMDSS radio maintainer. Visual inspections, on-air checks and battery tests are operator tasks.

src.quote: including basic equipment adjustments as denoted in the knowledge requirements

all adjustments of radio installations, servicing, or maintenance of such installations that may affect the proper operation of the GMDSS station must be performed by, or under the immediate supervision and responsibility of, a qualified GMDSS radio maintainer

15C2.why: A ship may not leave port until it can perform all its distress and safety functions. Ships using shore-based maintenance must also test each GMDSS unit, verify its performance and note the results before leaving every port. Replacement equipment whose performance hasn't been verified or logged doesn't meet that standard.

src.quote: a ship must not depart from any port unless and until the ship is capable of performing all distress and safety functions
Each GMDSS equipment must be tested and performance verified and the results noted in the ship's record before departure from every port.

15C3.why: The person qualified as the GMDSS radio maintainer may also be one of the designated GMDSS radio operators, as long as they're licensed as an operator. The other statements are wrong: one maintainer (not two) is enough for at-sea maintenance, and maintenance must be done by or under a maintainer, not an operator.

src.quote: This person may be, but need not be, the person designated as GMDSS radio operator as specified in § 80.1073.

15C4.why: Adjustments or maintenance that may affect the proper operation of the GMDSS station must be done by, or under the immediate supervision of, a qualified GMDSS radio maintainer. Resetting breakers, replacing fuses, routine battery care and replacing paper are routine operator tasks.

src.quote: all adjustments of radio installations, servicing, or maintenance of such installations that may affect the proper operation of the GMDSS station must be performed by, or under the immediate supervision and responsibility of, a qualified GMDSS radio maintainer

15C5.why: Whatever maintenance methods a ship uses, it may not leave any port until it can perform all the GMDSS distress and safety functions. Carrying extra operators, or using shore-based maintenance plus duplication instead of carrying a maintainer, is allowed.

src.quote: Irrespective of the maintenance methods used, a ship must not depart from any port unless and until the ship is capable of performing all distress and safety functions as specified in § 80.1081.

15C6.why: The tools, spare parts and test equipment a ship carries should be those the manufacturer recommends for the maintenance methods the ship uses.

src.quote: Adequate tools, spare parts, and test equipment appropriate to the methods used by the ship as recommended by the manufacturer should be provided.

16C1.why: Part 80 requires GMDSS ships to carry at least two people holding GMDSS Radio Operator's Licenses. A GROL or Marine Radio Operator Permit doesn't qualify, and a Maintainer's license alone is for maintenance, not operating.

src.quote: Ships must carry at least two persons holding GMDSS Radio Operator's Licenses

16C2.why: Statement C is false. A record must be kept of all incidents connected with the radio service that appear important to safety of life at sea; there's no exception for communications your ship wasn't involved in. The others are true: two licensed operators are required, a maintainer may also be carried, and work may be done by an operator under a maintainer's immediate supervision.

src.quote: A record must be kept, as required by the Radio Regulations and § 80.409 (a), (b) and (e), of all incidents connected with the radiocommunication service which appear to be of importance to safety of life at sea.

16C3.why: At-sea adjustments, servicing or maintenance that may affect the station must be done by or under a qualified GMDSS radio maintainer. The licenses that qualify are the GMDSS Maintainer's License (DM) and the GMDSS Operator's/Maintainer's License (DB).

src.quote: (1) DM: GMDSS Maintainer's License;
(2) DB: GMDSS Operator's/Maintainer's License.

16C4.why: Statement A is false: a record must be kept of all incidents connected with the radio service that appear to be important to safety of life at sea. The others are true: a primary and a backup GMDSS operator must be designated, and maintenance at sea must be done by or under a qualified maintainer.

src.quote: A record must be kept, as required by the Radio Regulations and § 80.409 (a), (b) and (e), of all incidents connected with the radiocommunication service which appear to be of importance to safety of life at sea.
A qualified GMDSS radio operator must be designated to have primary responsibility for radiocommunications during distress incidents

16C5.why: The FCC's GMDSS rules require equipment based on the intended sea areas, the ability to send and respond to distress alerts, and at least two licensed GMDSS radio operators. The operator requirement is the same in every sea area, and equipment requirements grow, not shrink, in A3 and A4.

src.quote: as appropriate for the sea area of areas through which it will pass during its intended voyage
Ships must carry at least two persons holding GMDSS Radio Operator's Licenses

16C6.why: A ship that chooses at-sea maintenance must carry at least one qualified GMDSS radio maintainer, whatever its sea areas.

src.quote: must carry at least one person who qualifies as a GMDSS radio maintainer

17C1.why: Statement A is false: the reserve source of energy does not need to supply independent HF and MF installations at the same time. The others are true: there must always be enough power to run the radios and charge the reserve batteries, a UPS must protect GMDSS equipment, and position input must survive a main or emergency power failure.

src.quote: The reserve sources of energy need not supply independent HF and MF radio installations at the same time.
An uninterruptible power supply or other means of ensuring a continuous supply of electrical power, within equipment tolerances, shall be provided to all GMDSS equipment

17C2.why: Reserve battery charge should be checked at least every 30 days, with the equipment on and the battery charger off, and the result logged.

src.quote: Battery charge levels should be checked at intervals of 30 days or less with equipment turned ON and the battery charger turned OFF.

17C3.why: The Reserve Source of Energy (RSE) powers the radio installations for distress and safety communications if both the ship's main and emergency sources of electrical power fail. The emergency or standby generators are the sources it backs up.

src.quote: A reserve source of energy to supply radio installations must be provided on every ship for the purpose of conducting distress and safety radiocommunications, in the event of failure of the ship's main and emergency sources of electrical power.

17C4.why: The reserve source of energy must be independent of the ship's propelling power and of the ship's electrical system, so it still works when ship's power is lost. It doesn't have to supply separate MF and HF installations at the same time.

src.quote: The reserve sources of energy must be independent of the propelling power of the ship and the ship's electrical system.

17C5.why: GMDSS ships normally have an emergency source of electrical power (a SOLAS requirement) and, in addition, a reserve source of energy that runs the radios if both the main and emergency sources fail. One doesn't replace the other, and a second EPIRB doesn't substitute for either.
17C5.note: Part 80 allows for some ships built before February 1, 1995, and cargo ships under 500 gross tons, that have no fully compliant emergency source. If so, their reserve source must last six hours instead of one.

src.quote: A reserve source of energy to supply radio installations must be provided on every ship
in the event of failure of the ship's main and emergency sources of electrical power
Six hours, on ships constructed before February 1, 1995, and on cargo ships of less than 500 tons gross tonnage, if the emergency source of electrical power is not provided or does not comply fully

17C6.why: The Reserve Source of Energy (RSE) is the back-up that runs the radio installations for distress and safety communications when the ship's main and emergency power sources fail. The other names are made up.

src.quote: A reserve source of energy to supply radio installations must be provided on every ship for the purpose of conducting distress and safety radiocommunications, in the event of failure of the ship's main and emergency sources of electrical power.

18C1.why: GMDSS equipment, including the VHF-DSC installation, must be tested daily at sea, and the satisfactory tests must be logged every day. A daily log entry on the condition of the required radiotelephone equipment is also needed.

src.quote: Daily entries of satisfactory tests to ensure the continued proper functioning of GMDSS equipment shall be made.
A daily statement about the condition of the required radiotelephone equipment, as determined by either normal communication or test communication;

18C2.why: Statement A is false. Coast Guard stations may be called on 2182 kHz or Channel 16 for tests only in limited cases, such as by FCC inspectors or technicians, so it isn't the right way to do a routine test. The others are true: normal traffic can count as the daily check, and a test must not interfere with traffic and must stop if a station says "wait".

src.quote: U.S. Coast Guard stations may be contacted on 2182 kHz or 156.800 MHz for test purposes only when tests are being conducted by Commission employees
as determined by either normal communication or test communication
The operator must not interfere with transmissions in progress.

18C3.why: GMDSS equipment, including the DSC controller, must be tested daily at sea, with a log entry each day. On top of that, a weekly log entry must confirm that the DSC equipment was verified by an actual call or a test call.

src.quote: Daily entries of satisfactory tests to ensure the continued proper functioning of GMDSS equipment shall be made.
The proper functioning of digital selective calling (DSC) equipment has been verified by actual communications or a test call;

18C4.why: At sea, the required equipment must be shown to work every day, either by a test or by successful use in normal communications. Survival craft equipment is checked on a different schedule (weekly log entries and tests at least every 12 months).

src.quote: A daily statement about the condition of the required radiotelephone equipment, as determined by either normal communication or test communication;
Daily entries of satisfactory tests to ensure the continued proper functioning of GMDSS equipment shall be made.
The portable survival craft radio gear and radar transponders have been tested

96J1.why: Rule of thumb: shorter distances call for lower frequencies, and daytime calls for higher frequencies (the ionosphere is more strongly ionized by day).

96J2.why: The HF rules of thumb: longer distance, higher frequency; shorter distance, lower frequency; daytime, higher frequency; nighttime, lower frequency.

96J3.why: San Francisco to Taiwan or the Philippines is a very long path, so use high HF bands (16 or 22 MHz) when both ends are in daylight, and drop to about 8 MHz when both ends are dark.

96J4.why: For routine band selection, distance and time of day matter most, then the season, then the sunspot cycle. Solar flares are occasional events you react to.

96J5.why: For routine work, the propagation rules of thumb (plus listening and past experience) are usually enough. Calculating MUF and similar figures isn't normal practice.

96J6.why: Use the propagation rules of thumb, or what has worked before on similar paths and times. Blind trial and error wastes time, and GMDSS operators aren't expected to rely on equipment-calculated optimum frequencies.

97J1.why: 16 MHz works well for long daylight paths. As evening comes, ionization drops and the band closes, so communications fade and become impossible at night. Switch to a lower band.

97J2.why: 4 MHz over about 350 miles is limited by daytime absorption. As evening comes, absorption falls and the signal improves, typically peaking at night and in the early morning.

97J3.why: At mid-day over about 1,800 miles, the higher HF bands work best. Lower bands are absorbed by day, and MF and VHF can't cover that distance.

97J4.why: At midnight over about 800 miles, an HF band is needed (a lower one, since it's night). VHF and UHF are line of sight.

97J5.why: 75 miles at mid-day is MF ground-wave territory: MF reaches about 100 miles, VHF only 20–30 miles, and 16 or 22 MHz skywave skips over short distances.

99J1.why: A fully charged lead-acid cell is about 2.1 volts.

99J2.why: A fully charged lead-acid cell has a specific gravity of about 1.265, measured with a hydrometer. A voltmeter measures voltage, not electrolyte density.

src.quote: including specific gravity of lead-acid storage batteries

99J3.why: Gel cells are sealed lead-acid batteries with gelled electrolyte. They need no topping up but may need specific charging rates and voltages, so use a charger suited to them.

99J4.why: In a series string, if one cell becomes weaker than the rest during discharge, the current from the other cells can drive it into reverse, effectively charging it in reverse polarity.

99J5.why: Specific gravity readings fall as temperature rises (warm electrolyte is less dense), so hydrometer readings are temperature-corrected.

99J6.why: On a 24 V system, a voltage briefly up near 30 V while the batteries recharge after a test is normal. A constant 30 V reading suggests the charger is stuck at a high charge voltage, which will overcharge the batteries.
